title: National anniversary participation is organized more through family, community, learning, and stories than official ceremony alone
source_unit: With Honor and Gallup survey of US adults about planned recognition of the nation's 250th anniversary

denominator.unit: US adults surveyed; article reports published shares without exposing the full unweighted denominator

any_planned_celebration.unit: percent of US adults planning to celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary in some way

family_friends.unit: percent among adults planning to celebrate, intending to spend time with family or friends

community_event.unit: percent among adults planning to celebrate, intending to participate in a neighborhood or community event

official_program.unit: percent among adults planning to celebrate, intending to attend an official America250 program

media_following.unit: percent among adults planning to celebrate, intending to follow anniversary coverage on television or social media

observations.method: With Honor/Gallup descriptive survey of planned anniversary recognition; activities are separate, nonexclusive intentions rather than observed participation.
observations.uncertainty: Plans do not establish attendance, conversation, learning, service, political action, or durable national identity; activity denominators are article-specific.
observations.subgroup: US adults, with age and party comparisons reported separately.
observations.counterinterpretation: Family or community celebration can be social ritual without political agreement, and official-program nonattendance does not imply civic withdrawal.

observations.period: May 12-22, 2026; educational and civic forms of recognition

denominator.unit: percent of US adults planning to recognize the anniversary through civic or educational activities; article-reported subgroup

history_learning.unit: percent among adults in the civic/educational recognition subgroup

personal_stories.unit: percent among adults in the civic/educational recognition subgroup, intending to listen to personal stories or perspectives

domestic_travel.unit: percent among adults in the civic/educational recognition subgroup

service_or_charity.unit: percent among adults in the civic/educational recognition subgroup

culture_or_arts.unit: percent among adults in the civic/educational recognition subgroup

observations.method: Descriptive activity comparison among respondents who said they planned a civic or educational form of recognition; activities are nonexclusive intentions.
observations.uncertainty: The measure captures intended meaning-making routes but not whether people completed them, learned something, changed views, or formed new relationships.
observations.subgroup: US adults reporting planned civic or educational anniversary recognition.
observations.counterinterpretation: History learning and personal-story listening can reinforce existing identities as well as create common ground; planned service may be symbolic or practical.

observations.period: May 12-22, 2026; sources of national pride and future optimism

denominator.unit: US adults surveyed; source reports multiple-choice sources of pride and optimism

pride_freedoms.unit: percent selecting Americans' freedoms as a top source of pride

pride_diversity.unit: percent selecting the country's diversity as a top source of pride

pride_hard_work_opportunity.unit: percent selecting opportunities to work hard and improve circumstances as a top source of pride

any_future_optimism.unit: percent identifying at least one reason for optimism about the nation's future

optimism_stand_up.unit: percent selecting people's willingness to stand up for what they believe is right as a top reason for optimism

observations.method: Descriptive multiple-choice survey measures with age and party comparisons; pride and optimism are meaning judgments, not institutional performance indicators.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not establish what respondents do because of these meanings, whether views persist, or whether they imply agreement about history, policy, or national institutions.
observations.subgroup: US adults overall, with age and party comparisons.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared pride categories can conceal disagreement about what freedoms, diversity, opportunity, or standing up mean in practice.

boundary: This record establishes planned national-anniversary participation, social and educational ritual routes, and sources of pride and optimism. It does not establish actual attendance, cross-party agreement, historical learning, civic capacity, policy support, institutional trust, or durable political action.
